documents.title: EUGOGO 2021 clinical practice guidelines for medical management of Graves orbitopathy

chunks.content: Thyroid-associated ophthalmopathy (TAO, AKA thyroid eye disease) represents a presumed autoimmune process closely associated with Graves’ disease (GD) . Not a scintilla of convincing evidence to date has been advanced demonstrating that the immunological makeup of individuals with GD and manifesting TAO are fundamentally distinct from those without periocular disease. In fact, many workers in the field advocate the view that all patients with bono fide GD have some measure of TAO, although it might be subclinical in severity. In the past, treatment options for TAO have been limited to relatively nonspecific agents with multiple off-target side effects. Most notable among these are glucocorticoid steroids, administered locally or systemically , . This reliance on medications unproven by adequate placebo-controlled trials and all of which were unapproved for TAO was necessitated by the pervasive uncertainty surrounding root mechanisms underlying TAO. While the molecular events leading to its development remain incompletely understood, the pathology, natural disease course and clinical consequences of TAO have been described in great detail. Understanding its pathogenesis is evolving as more information comes to light. These insights are frequently accomplished by borrowing investigative strategies gathered during the study of other autoimmune diseases. Better definition of disease mechanisms has allowed development of targeted therapies. Thus, the historical reliance on treatments remaining relatively untested can now give way to a more enlightened approach to patient care. In this review, I attempt to describe many of the most consequential discoveries made over the past few decades concerning TAO and leading to currently available therapy. Given its relative brevity, mention of some important studies may have been omitted. Is TAO a local disease or merely a localized manifestation of a systemic process? Striking concordance between the development of TAO and autoimmune thyroid diseases, more commonly with GD and less frequently with Hashimoto’s thyroiditis, strongly suggests that these processes are intimately intertwined. Many investigators exploring the pathogenesis of TAO and caring for patients with the disease focus almost entirely on local orbital processes rather than considering the systemic events that appear to underlie them. The etiologic basis for TAO remains inadequately explored and the vast emphasis of treatment has focused on orbital tissues. Pathological events occurring within the professional immune system may represent more important therapeutic targets, potentially providing more than a treatment “band aid”. These include loss of immune tolerance within both the central (bone marrow and thymus) and peripheral (tolerogenic dendritic cells, regulatory T cells, among others) immune systems. Thus, therapies simply targeting the orbital tissues may succeed in transiently dampening localized manifestations (inflammation, tissue edema, pain, etc) rather than alleviating their root causes. Genetic and acquired factors promoting GD and TAO Identity of instigating factors underlying development of GD and TAO has alluded the scientific community. A genetic basis for disease susceptibility appears to be layered upon as yet uncertain environmental/acquired factor(s). Several genetic signatures remain candidates as the basis for susceptibility to GD. ( , ) Polymorphisms of TSH receptor (TSHR), CTLA-4, CD25, thyroglobulin, HLA-DRβ-Arg74, CD40 and PTPN22 are among these. An open question concerns whether genetic determinants for GD might differ from those for TAO. To date, no convincing evidence has been advanced suggesting that genetic and nongenetic risk factors for the two disease manifestations differ. A recent study demonstrated significant associations between TAO and HLA profiles such as HLAA*01:01, -A*32:01, -B*37:01, -B*39:01, -B*42:01, -C*08:02, C*03:02, DRB1*03:01, DRB1*14:01 and DQB1*02:01.( ) In contrast, HLA-C*04:01, -C*03:04, -C*07:02 and -DRB1*15:02 appear to represent protective alleles. Epigenetic factors could also account for disease development and the heterogeneous presentations of GD and TAO. It remains a mystery why only 10–30% of patients with thyroid-centric GD develop clinically meaningful TAO. Altered methylation of genes encoding TSHR and several T cell (Tc) signaling molecules has been detected in GD, but these patterns do not appear to differ in patients without TAO compared to those with it. ( ) Alternatively, the medley of disease-associated signaling pathways and genes, the expression and activities of which are altered in thyroid and orbital tissues, could ultimately explain whether individual patients with GD manifest TAO. In addition to genetic and epigenetic factors, “psychic triggers” have long been considered as potentially explaining the sudden onset of GD and perhaps TAO ( – ). Specific antecedent events are frequently associated with developing thyroid dysfunction and ocular manifestations. These include physical stress such as serious injury, myocardial infarction and undergoing major surgery. Personal loss and incarceration represent examples of emotional trauma invoked as causative in some patients. Tobacco smoking and large iodine intake can also increase risk. ( – ) Treatment with the anti-CD52 medication, alemtuzumab, for chronic lymphocytic leukemia and multiple sclerosis has been linked to the onset of thyroid autoimmunity, especially GD without or with TAO. ( , ) Thus multiple exogenous factors have been implicated as potentially triggering GD

( , ) Thus multiple exogenous factors have been implicated as potentially triggering GD and TAO. ( , ) Recent interest in selenium as a dietary constituent and its deficiency as an independent risk in GD has led some workers in the field to advocate dietary supplementation in virtually all patients with these diseases. ( , ) Involvement of the professional immune system in TAO Normal immune responses, such as those elicited in host defense against infections, cancer and mechanical/thermal injury, involve a complex interplay between elements of innate immunity (such as monocytes, dendritic cells, basophils, eosinophils, mast cells, Langerhans cells, macrophages, neutrophils and NK cells) and the two major cellular components of adaptive immunity, Tc and B cells (Bc) ( ). Immune reactivity within the TAO orbit resembles that occurring in other autoimmune diseases (such as rheumatoid arthritis, psoriasis, etc) and is likely similar or identical to that occurring within the GD thyroid gland. Both Tc and Bc have been implicated convincingly in the development of TAO by virtue of their documented presence in the diseased orbit. Lymphocytes are present, often in high abundance, relatively early in the orbital disease course but may be absent or sparse later in the disease course. They have been partially characterized, but whether a subpopulation within the orbit is antigen specific has yet to be established. ( – ) Effector and regulatory cells of both lineages are among the infiltrating cells in active TAO. Tc and Bc endorse each other as they participate in multiple immune processes. Balance between these cell populations is thought to determine amplitude of disease activity and magnitude of severity. Some of the abnormalities identified in lymphocytes might be attributed to IGF-IR over-expression in both Tc and Bc. ( , ) This IGF-IR over-expression carries functional consequences. Besides lymphocytes, mast cells have also been identified in affected orbital connective tissues and have been shown to interact directly with TAO orbital fibroblasts (GD-OF), altering the patterns of gene expression in those cells. ( – ) Monocytes and their derivatives, including macrophages, can be detected locally in active TAO. In aggregate, these immune cells generate a substantial array of cytokines which in concert with molecules generated by GD-OF, appear to determine the clinical behavior of TAO. They therefore influence greatly the pattern of tissue reactivity and remodeling. In addition to cytokines, several chemokines and chemoattractants promote the infiltration of “second wave” cell participants into the orbit. In theory, some of these could amplify tissue disruption while others might play largely regulatory/reparative roles in these tissues and therefore facilitate and hasten disease resolution. Tc and Bc can engage in cross-talk with GD-OF by virtue of many costimulatory factors and their cognate receptors. Among these are several molecular bridges such as CD40/CD40L (CD154), growth factors and cytokines. These pathways and the signaling they mediate represent candidate therapeutic targets. The putative role of CD40/CD154 playing an important role in GD and TAO derives from the expression pattern of functional CD40 in thyroid epithelium and orbital fibroblasts. ( , ) Cross-talk between Tc and GD-OF can also occur through a variety of cytokine networks. ( , ) These interactions appear to drive inductions of specific genes in TAO. ( , , ) Besides IL-1β, IL-4, IL-6, and TGF-β, IL-17A appears to participate in the development of TAO ( ) through its upregulation of RANTES. Further, genetically driven CD40 overexpression may represent an increased disease susceptibility.( ) Antigen presenting cells in TAO The search for candidate antigen presenting cells (APCs) within the orbit and potentially involved in TAO has included examining multiple cell-types, including monocytes, macrophages and dendritic cells (Dc). Intra-orbital Dc have yet to be detected in TAO. Bc also present antigens ( ) and thus these cells remain candidates once they have infiltrated the orbit. GD-OF were studied for their potential as APCs, dating back to early studies reporting that interferon γ can induce HLA DR expression more robustly in these fibroblasts than those from healthy donors (H-OF) ( ) and that glucocorticoids can attenuate this induction. ( ) Evidence for the thyrotropin receptor playing a role in TAO Thyrotropin receptor (TSHR) represents the central autoantigen in GD. ( ) Activating anti-TSHR autoantibodies are both pathognomonic for GD and specifically drive the characteristic thyroidal disturbances in the disease.

( ) Evidence for the thyrotropin receptor playing a role in TAO Thyrotropin receptor (TSHR) represents the central autoantigen in GD. ( ) Activating anti-TSHR autoantibodies are both pathognomonic for GD and specifically drive the characteristic thyroidal disturbances in the disease. ( ) Parmentier et al ( ) were the first to molecularly clone the TSHR gene. This was followed shortly thereafter by Feliciello et al ( ) who reported identifying TSHR transcripts at extremely low levels in orbital fat. Subsequently TSHR mRNA was detected in multiple fat deposits outside the orbit. ( ) The seemingly ubiquitous expression of TSHR implies the potential for that receptor to play physiological roles throughout the human body. It has been conjectured that abnormal expression of TSHR within the thymus, perhaps genetically determined, may underlie the pathogenesis of GD. ( ) GD-OF were among the first cultured cell types found to express TSHR transcripts peripheral to the thyroid gland. ( ) Further, GD-OF express somewhat higher levels of the receptor than do those detected in H-OF. Subsequent studies revealed that the protein expressed in GD-OF and H-OF is functional since both TSH and GD-IgG can induce specific gene expression (and in CD34 + fibrocytes, which is described later). These include IL-1 receptor antagonist and IL-6. ( , ) The potential role of DNA methylation in determining how orbital fibroblasts respond to TSH was examined recently. ( ) The authors of that report found that DNA methylation of many genes in both H-OF and GD-OF was increased following treatment with M22, a TSHR agonistic monoclonal antibody cloned from a patient with GD. ( ) Among the methylated genes examined was that encoding IGF-IR. Levels of TSHR expression are upregulated by IGF-I. ( ) Besides the induction of cytokine expression, TSH enhances orbital fibroblast proliferation, actions mediated through PI3K and Akt signaling and induction of miR-146 and miR-155. ( ) Insinuation of IGF-IR in the pathogenesis of TAO Relatedness of the IGF-I pathway to thyroid physiology dates back to the experimental observations of Ingbar and colleagues who reported that both insulin and IGF-I could enhance the actions of TSH and GD-IgG on thyroid epithelial cells. ( ) These investigators began to tease apart the intersection of effects on cell proliferation of TSH and IGF-I; however, the details of molecular interplay between the respective signaling pathways had yet to be identified. Later, Weightman and colleagues described the ability of GD-IgG to displace radiolabeled IGF-I from the then unidentified binding sites on the surface of orbital fibroblasts. ( ) That binding site was later identified as IGF-IR and its signaling properties and involvement in responses to GD-IgG were characterized several years thereafter. ( , ) Directly relevant to TAO, GD-IgG was shown to induce the expression of two powerful chemoattractants in GD-OF, namely IL-16 (a CD4-specific ligand) and “regulated upon activation, normal T cell expressed and presumably secreted” (RANTES). Critically, those studies identified the necessary role of IGF-IR in transducing the cellular responses to rhTSH and GD-IgG and the resulting activation of downstream target genes. They brought to light inherent differences in responses elicited in GD-OF compared to H-OF. ( – ) Subsequently, it was determined that the levels of IGF-IR expression in TAO Tc and Bc as well as GD-OF were considerably higher than in those respective cell types derived from healthy individuals. ( , , ) Moreover, abnormal IGF-IR signaling in these cells was found to have functional consequences in each. The importance of β-arrestins in the interactions between IGF-IR and TSHR has illuminated a number of potentially important aspects of pathogenic signaling initiated by autoantibodies in GD and TAO (reviewed recently by Girnita et al ). ( ) Subsequent studies conducted in vitro revealed that IGF-IR inhibition can result in attenuation of responses to TSH, IGF-I and GD-IgG in CD34 + fibrocytes. ( ) Teprotumumab, a fully human IGF-IR-specific monoclonal antibody inhibitor, can attenuate both basal and TSH-dependent expression of Bc activating factor (BAFF), thyroglobulin, TSHR, sodium iodide symporter, thyroperoxidase, and IL-10 in CD34 + fibrocytes. ( ) It can enhance levels of IL-12p35, both intracellular and secreted IL-1 receptor antagonist, and Slit2 while downregulating IL-23p19. The small molecule IGF-IR tyrosine kinase inhibitor, linisitinib, can mimic the effects of teprotumumab. In contrast, teprotumumab fractionally enhances the synthesis of hyaluronan in GD-OF through an upregulation of HAS2 levels. In contrast, teprotumumab fractionally enhances the synthesis of hyaluronan in GD-OF through an upregulation of HAS2 levels. Fibroblasts from the TAO orbit GD-OF, initially characterized by Sisson and colleagues, ( , ) are widely considered the major cellular effectors in the TAO orbit. ( ) Despite substantial evidence to the contrary, GD-OF are frequently considered as monolithic and investigated as representing a homogeneous cell population rather than as a mixture of fibroblastic cells exhibiting substantially divergent phenotypic attributes. ( , ) The vast majority of studies on GD-OF have failed to examine the cellular characteristics of subsetted cells based on specific markers, potentially obscuring the important cellular attributes of each fibroblast subtype. The heterogeneity of GD-OF cultures was initially found to comprise both Thy-1 + (AKA CD90) and Thy-1 − cells displaying similar morphologies and growth characteristics. ( ) Soon thereafter, initial attempts at studying pure cell subsets of primary cultures yielded insights into the divergent capacities of Thy-1 + and Thy-1 − cells to undergo differentiation. The Thy-1 + phenotype possesses the capacity to differentiate into myofibroblasts when exposed to TGF-β. In contrast, Thy-1 − GD-OF more readily differentiate into adipocytes when activated through the proliferator-activated receptor γ pathway. ( , ) Thus, it would appear that GD-OF represent a heterogeneous population of cells based on Thy-1 surface display and that this heterogeneity carries functional and disease susceptibility implications. Emergence of CD34<sup>+</sup> fibrocyte involvement in TAO and comprising GD-OF subpopulations An additional cellular characteristic, the basis of which allowed further segregation of mixed populations of GD-OF, emerged following identification of CD34 + CXCR4 + Collagen 1 + cells in the parental strains of GD-OF. ( ) These cells appear to represent infiltrating CD34 + fibrocytes that masquerade in the TAO orbit as cells morphologically similar to residential CD34 − OF. ( ) Fibrocytes have an established role in tissue remodeling, fibrosis and wound healing. ( ) They have been implicated in multiple autoimmune diseases including scleroderma and rheumatoid arthritis. ( ) These cells can efficiently present antigens to Tc by virtue of their display of B7 costimulatory molecules and MHC II. ( ) They can be readily identified by their retention of molecular markers including CD34, CXCR4 and collagen 1. Like their putative progenitors, circulating fibrocytes coming from the bone marrow, they express relatively high levels of TSHR, establishing their potential relevance in TAO and GD. ( ) In addition to TSHR, fibrocytes express thyroperoxidase, functional thyroglobulin, and sodium iodide symporter. ( , ) The expression of these proteins by fibrocytes seems to rely on the autoimmune regulator protein (AIRE), a noncanonical transcription factor involved in thymic Tc education. Interrogation of CD34 + OF have revealed that these cells, like fibrocytes, also express thyroid-associated molecules but at substantially lower levels of protein and encoding mRNAs. It appears that once these cells infiltrate the orbit and become tissue cohabitants with CD34 − OF, their switching from high to low level expression of these molecules is the consequence, at least in part, of Slit2 coming from CD34 − OF. Slit2 appears to downregulate specific gene expression at both the transcriptional and post-transcriptional levels. ( ) An as yet unresolved issue concerns whether endogenous or extrinsic factors determine whether fibrocytes contribute to the development of TAO, either as effectors (promoting disease) or as players with a largely regulatory role (dampening disease). Circulating fibrocytes from patients manifesting TAO express higher levels of TSHR than do those from healthy individuals and those with GD but without TAO. CD34 + fibrocytes have substantial capacity for presenting antigens in a variety of physiological and pathological contexts. ( ) This is likely true while they are infiltrating tissue niches or in circulation. Thus, fibrocytes may represent an important component of immune response in TAO. Slit2, an enforcer of fibrocyte civility and molecular tranquility? Slit2, a neuronal axon repellent glycoprotein, is expressed and released from CD34 − OF. It was first identified for its importance in enforcing midline integrity during CNS development. ( ) Slit2 has been shown to inhibit fibrocyte differentiation, thereby modulating fibrosis in lung tissue. ( ) It acts through its cognate receptor, roundabout 1 (ROBO1).( ) CD34 + fibrocytes express ROBO1 and when engaged by Slit2, this receptor is activated, resulting in down regulation of TSHR, Tg, TPO, and NIS levels. Slit2, a neuronal axon repellent glycoprotein, is expressed and released from CD34 − OF. It was first identified for its importance in enforcing midline integrity during CNS development. ( ) Slit2 has been shown to inhibit fibrocyte differentiation, thereby modulating fibrosis in lung tissue. ( ) It acts through its cognate receptor, roundabout 1 (ROBO1).( ) CD34 + fibrocytes express ROBO1 and when engaged by Slit2, this receptor is activated, resulting in down regulation of TSHR, Tg, TPO, and NIS levels. ( ) These inhibitory effects on gene expression are apparently mediated through the downregulation of AIRE. In addition, Slit2 enhances IL-12 expression while attenuating that of IL-23 through action on gene transcription levels. ( ) Slit2 upregulates HAS2, increasing the production of hyaluronan in GD-OFs. ( ) Thus, Slit2 appears to support HA synthesis in certain cell types. Current therapeutic landscape for TAO: an expanding role for medical intervention? Given the broadening insights into TAO pathogenesis, several candidate molecular targets for medical intervention have been identified recently, based on experimental inquiry leading to increased plausibility ( ). Thus, for the first time, targeted therapy has emerged from near-complete reliance on nonspecific agents. As mentioned earlier, the majority of nonsurgical therapy for TAO, specifically timed during the inflammatory, progressive phase, has involved use of either local or systemic glucocorticoid steroids. ( ) Considerable debate continues to rage over the wisdom of continuing the use of steroids in light of newer, more targeted agents. ( ) While several European experts have long advocated steroids as the “gold standard” medical therapy, recent evidence indicates that the majority of North American physicians treating TAO do not use these agents routinely. ( ) Further, only a single trial, involving 15 patients with moderate to severe TAO, has been reported as placebo controlled. The authors of that study ( ) concluded steroid superiority over placebo based on responses heavily weighted toward inflammation-related signs and symptoms over 48-week observation. Methylprednisolone (6g total) was administered over 3 months in 6 patients compared with 9 patients receiving placebo. Importantly, response in reducing proptosis and improving diplopia was not essential for achieving primary response in this study. A more recent approach, based on a single published trial not reaching its primary endpoint, concluded that the combination of high-dosage pulse steroids and mycophenolate might be superior to steroids as single agents. ( ) Remarkably, this combination therapy has been touted as “first line” therapy for moderate-to-severe TAO in the recently published EUGOGO guidelines. ( ) The recommendation has been challenged based on the inadequate evidence supporting its use. ( ) A statement including mycophenolate as first line therapy for TED is not included in the even more recently published joint statement from the European-American Thyroid Association. ( ) Birth of teprotumumab for the treatment of TAO Teprotumumab, a fully human IgG1 monoclonal antibody IGF-IR inhibitor, was developed by Roche as a therapy for solid cancers. The program at Roche was paralleled by those of several other pharmaceutical companies, each with their own molecule targeting IGF-IR. After outcomes of several clinical trials were analyzed, these developmental programs were curtailed for lack of efficacy, including that of teprotumumab. Importantly, these studies of IGF-IR inhibitors for cancer, conducted in the 2000’s, ( ) revealed that these drugs were generally well-tolerated with encouraging safety profiles. Teprotumumab was evaluated in two placebo-controlled, double masked, multi- institutional clinical trials in adult patients (18–80 years) with TAO judged to manifest active, short-duration (<9 mos from development) and moderate to severe disease. ( , ) Unlike the standards usually adhered to in judging responses to steroids and other anti-inflammatory agents in TAO, those two studies of teprotumumab included a necessary reduction in proptosis ≥ 2mm in the more seriously affected eye to reach primary response. In addition, improvement in diplopia was also widely observed. More detailed accounting of these clinical responses can be found in recent primary reports and reviews found elsewhere ( , – ) and in other contributions to this collection of papers (Strianese and Pakdel). Several adverse events had emerged from the two clinical trials of teprotumumab, notably including hyperglycemia and auditory abnormalities. It should be anticipated that glucose excursions would occur in patients treated with an IGF-IR inhibitor, given the role of IGF-IR in maintaining normal glucose metabolism. Hyperglycemia developing as the consequence of treatment with teprotumumab has been attributed to several different mechanisms including alterations in gluconeogenesis ( ) and the physical and functional associations occurring between IGF-IR and insulin receptors. ( , ) In fact, most insulin receptor molecules exist as chimeric proteins, associating with IGF-IR. Because these two “half-receptors” interplay functionally, inhibiting IGF-IR most likely results in relative insulin resistance. These and other AEs have been described in detail previously. ( ) Mechanisms involved in clinical responses to teprotumumab <italic toggle="yes">in vivo</italic> The question of how and in which tissues clinically consequential IGF-IR inhibition might be occurring in mediating responses to teprotumumab remains uncertain. Within the orbit, GD-OF express IGF-IR in a physical and functional complex with TSHR in situ .( ) A stimulating TSHR antibody induces IGF-1R phosphorylation and can initiate both TSHR and IGF-1R signaling in fibroblasts from “mice and men”. 1H7, a murine IGF-IR inhibitor monoclonal antibody was found to inhibit multiple IGF-IR signaling cascades and reduce TSHR signaling. ( ) A recent study demonstrated that inhibiting IGF-IR in GD-OF in vitro resulted in “suppressing IGF-1R signaling leading to retro-orbital fibroblast/adipocyte death through the cell-extrinsic pathway of apoptosis”. ( ) That report demonstrated that IGF-IR inhibition can suppress several proteins, including Beclin1, LC3a, LC3b, p62, and ULK1 in GD-OF, all related to autophagy while inducing apoptosis-related proteins, including caspase 3 activation, FADD, and caspase 8. Further the authors state that “This is likely the major mechanism involved in proptosis reduction in patients with Graves’ eye disease treated by IGF-1R inhibition”. ( )Their conclusions may be correct, given the earlier studies demonstrating direct effects of IGF-IR inhibition (1H7, teprotumumab, lisitinib) on GD-OF and CD34 + fibrocytes, but the authors failed to consider information provided in another study which has revealed a very different possibility. That report, by Fernando et al ( ) demonstrated consequences of in vivo actions of teprotumumab in patients treated with teprotumumab. Flow cytometric analysis of peripheral blood mononuclear cells from treated patients with moderate to severe TAO, collected at baseline and following treatment per study protocol ( ) with teprotumumab over 24 weeks, demonstrated substantial reductions in cell surface displayed CD80/CD86, PD-L1, and MHC II levels in CD34 + CXCR4 + fibrocytes. These attenuated protein levels were significant when compared to baseline in paired analysis (p<0.0001). In contrast, levels of these molecules in placebo-treated patients failed to undergo change. Analysis of CD4 + Tc from patients receiving teprotumumab also revealed substantial reductions in IL-17A and IFNγ levels in vivo . Companion studies conducted in vitro disclosed that the effects of teprotumumab were mediated at both transcriptional and mRNA stability. Importantly, IGF-IR inhibition and Slit2 share several consequences, suggesting the possibility that teprotumumab, and perhaps other IGF-IR inhibitors, might act through intermediate effects on endogenous Slit2 activity. In fact, Slit2 and ROBO1, its cognate receptor, were found to be upregulated by teprotumumab in GD-OF. ( ) Potential for increasingly more effective TAO therapies Like virtually all medical therapies for vexing, complex diseases, despite the impressive and unprecedented clinical responses to teprotumumab and the generally well-tolerated attributes of that drug, ineffectiveness in some patients and relatively infrequent side effects invite further treatment improvements. Recent consensus guidance has been provided by a group of ophthalmologists who treat TAO. ( ) Clearly those experts consider use of teprotumumab in a subset of patients to be appropriate. As they and others have noted, the drug is associated with side effects and some patients fail to respond adequately to the 8-infusion treatment protocol frequently employed. Thus, that realization has provoked an ongoing quest for perfection. Multiple molecules targeting IGF-IR are under development and additional therapeutic targets are being considered. Among these are VRDN (another anti-IGF-IR monoclonal antibody) and linisitinib, a small molecule tyrosine kinase inhibitor. Among the more promising and plausible of the alternative therapeutic targets is TSHR, the blockade of which in theory could directly treat the thyroid glandular hyperactivity frequently accompanying GD as well as TAO ( ). Development of molecules acting at TSHR continue. Both monoclonal antibodies and small molecules are currently in the developmental pipeline. ( , ) Another potential target is the CD40/CD154 pathway. more promising and plausible of the alternative therapeutic targets is TSHR, the blockade of which in theory could directly treat the thyroid glandular hyperactivity frequently accompanying GD as well as TAO ( ). Development of molecules acting at TSHR continue. Both monoclonal antibodies and small molecules are currently in the developmental pipeline. ( , ) Another potential target is the CD40/CD154 pathway. This molecular bridge functions in the crosstalk occurring between Tc and Bc and with GD-OF. CD40/CD154 (CD40 ligand) has been therapeutically targeted in other autoimmune diseases. By virtue of their high level CD40 expression, both GD-OF and thyroid epithelial cells can respond to CD154 with induction of IL-6, IL-8, prostaglandin endoperoxide H synthase 2 expression and hyaluronan synthesis. CFZ533, an anti-CD40 blocking monoclonal antibody ( ), was tested in a clinical trial of hyperthyroid patients with GD. Nearly 50% of patients treated with the molecule responded by becoming biochemical euthyroid. ( ) Tocilizumab is a blocking monoclonal antibody directed against the IL-6 receptor and has found a niche in the treatment paradigm of several autoimmune diseases including rheumatoid arthritis (RA), giant cell arteritis, and polyarticular and systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis. ( ) Satralizumab also targets the IL-6 receptor and was recently approved by the FDA for the treatment of neuromyelitis optica. ( ) Tocilizumab has been evaluated recently, primarily in studies centered in Spain in patients resistant to steroids. ( ) Whether IL-6 receptor blockade can result in clinically meaningful reduction of proptosis and/or diplopia in TAO remains uncertain. Critical in the regulation of circulating serum albumin levels and immunoglobulin clearance is the neonatal fragment crystallizable receptor (FcRn). It links these molecules to the lysosomal pathways. Disrupting FcRn-IgG interactions by therapeutically targeting the receptor with monoclonal antibodies can accelerate disposal of pathogenic autoantibodies. Myasthenia gravis is among the diseases for which this approach has been taken. RVT-1401 and HBM9161 represent two monoclonal antibodies thus far being explored for the treatment of GD and TAO. Potential drawbacks to this therapeutic approach include its relative non-specificity and its entire focus on autoantibodies, potentially without altering the pathogenic roles of Tc in these diseases. The trial of RTV-1401, developed by Immunovant, was suspended after reports of drug-related hypercholesterolemia appeared. As of this writing, the trial of RTV-1401 has been restarted. It is thus clear that several strategies are under development for the treatment of TAO. Many appear to possess substantial plausibility based on known disease mechanisms but virtually all can also be associated with concerning adverse events. Recognition of the important signaling pathways and genes expressed by GD-OF and CD34+ fibrocytes has allowed several additional therapeutic targets to be considered. In my view, our ultimate goal should include the restoration of immune tolerance to pathogenic autoantigens underlying TAO. It is very possible that some of these antigenic molecules may remain unidentified. This aspirational goal in theory would spare patients exposure to medications impairing host defense against infections and cancer. Besides developing additional therapies, several other goals must be achieved. Predictive biomarkers are needed to stratify patients according to their risk for developing severe disease, identifying patients more likely to benefit from targeted therapy, and judging therapeutic responses. To date, no molecular signatures reliably delineate those patients with GD who are destined to develop TAO in the future.
